summary: Defines terms for benchmarking ATM switching devices that support Available Bit Rate service, and for reporting test results.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a word list for describing how well a data-moving machine shares the road when traffic changes.

questions: how do you measure abr switch performance
subtitle: Words for measuring how fast ATM switches can adapt to changing traffic.

tldr.problem: There was no standard way to measure and describe how well ATM switches handle Available Bit Rate traffic, and no consistent terminology for benchmarking these devices.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines precise terms for ABR performance benchmarks, including parameters that control how quickly switches adjust transmission rates and metrics that measure response times and error rates.
tldr.outcome: Network operators and equipment vendors can now use the same terminology when discussing ABR benchmarking results, improving interoperability and fair comparisons.

today: RFC 3134 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the standard reference for ABR benchmarking terminology, used by vendors and operators when comparing ATM switch performance.

sections.title: Introduction to ATM ABR Benchmarking
sections.content:
This RFC defines terminology for testing and measuring the performance of ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) switches that support ABR (Available Bit Rate) service. ABR is a way for networks to dynamically adjust how fast data flows based on how busy the network is.

The document builds on earlier benchmarking standards (RFCs 1242, 2285, 2544, and 2761) and adds ABR-specific terminology. Benchmarking is important because vendors and operators need a common language to compare equipment fairly and understand performance in real-world conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, people measured networks using different words, like speaking different languages. This document teaches everyone the same words for ATM so they can compare fairly.

sections.title: ABR Service Parameters
sections.content:
ABR uses several key parameters that control how switches and endpoints behave. Allowed Cell Rate (ACR) is the current rate at which a source can send, measured in cells per second. At startup, a source begins at Initial Cell Rate (ICR) and may decrease no lower than Minimum Cell Rate (MCR), which can be zero.

Peak Cell Rate (PCR) sets the maximum speed, and Additive Increase Rate (AIR) controls how quickly the rate can grow. The rate can decrease faster than it increases; Rate Decrease Factor (RDF) is a power of 2 ranging from 1/32,768 to 1.

Other parameters like Trm, Nrm, and ADTF control the timing and frequency of rate-adjustment signals. All of these directly affect TCP throughput and latency.
sections.plainLanguage: These are knobs on the network that say how fast to go, how slow to go, and when to check if the road is busy. Turning the knobs differently makes the network behave differently.

sections.title: Resource Management Cells
sections.content:
Resource Management (RM) cells are special short messages that carry information about network conditions between switches and endpoints. An RM cell contains an ATM header (5 bytes), a protocol ID (3 bytes), a function-specific field (45 bytes) with fields like Explicit Rate (ER), Congestion Indication (CI), and No Increase (NI), plus reserved space (6 bytes) and a CRC-10 error detection code (10 bytes).

The RM cell's total size is 66 bytes. Forward RM cells travel from source toward destination, and the destination turns them around as backward RM cells to send feedback. The Direction (DIR) bit toggles from 0 (forward) to 1 (backward) at the destination.
sections.plainLanguage: RM cells are tiny messages the network sends to say 'go faster' or 'slow down.' They travel both directions and include a safety check so the message doesn't get scrambled.

sections.title: Performance Metrics
sections.content:
The RFC defines metrics that measure how switches respond to changing traffic conditions. ABR Rate Increase Response Time (ARIRT) measures how long it takes a switch to increase its transmission rate after receiving a rate-increase request. Similarly, ABR Rate Decrease Response Time (ARDRT) is the time needed to decrease rate after a decrease request.

RM-Cell Transfer Delay (RM-CTD) is the time an RM cell takes to travel from source to destination. RM-Cell Delay Variation (RM-CDV) is the difference between the maximum and minimum transfer delays, which affects how quickly the source learns about network conditions.

Error metrics include RM-Cell Error Ratio (RM-CER), RM-Cell Loss Ratio (RM-CLR), and Severely Errored Cell Block Ratio (SECBR). All these metrics directly impact whether TCP connections through an ABR network perform well.
sections.plainLanguage: These are report cards that say how long feedback takes, how accurate it is, and how many messages get lost. Bad scores mean TCP slows down.

sections.title: Relationship to Other Benchmarking Work
sections.content:
This document complements four foundational RFCs: RFC 1242 defines general benchmarking terminology, RFC 2544 describes methodology for measuring interconnect devices, RFC 2285 covers LAN switching, and RFC 2761 provides general ATM benchmarking terms.

The terms in RFC 3134 do not redefine metrics already covered in these RFCs (such as CDV, CER, CLR, CMR, and CTD). Instead, they extend the vocabulary specifically for ABR. This organization allows readers to consult the appropriate RFC for their context without unnecessary duplication.
sections.plainLanguage: Other documents define measuring tools for networks. This one adds special words just for the ABR case, so people don't get confused.
